keyTakeaways: Halloween in Scotland is 31 October (Saturday in 2026, Sunday in 2027); Auld Hallowe'en, the Old Style date, is 11 November.
Guising means earning a treat with a party piece; the Scottish National Dictionary records guizards in Edinburgh in 1773.
Kail-pulling, a Halloween fortune game, appears in a 1736 Caithness church record, almost 50 years before Burns wrote 'Halloween' in 1785.
Paisley Halloween Festival runs 23 to 24 October 2026 with a 400-strong parade; Samhuinn burns on Edinburgh's Calton Hill on 31 October 2026.

faqs.question: What do Scottish children have to do when they go guising?
faqs.answer: They perform a party piece at each door, usually a short joke, a song or a rhyme, before the householder hands over a treat. The custom descends from guisers who acted short plays at Hogmanay, recorded as early as 1825.

faqs.question: What is a party piece at Halloween in Scotland?
faqs.answer: It is the small performance a guiser gives in exchange for sweets: a joke, a rhyme or a verse of a song. Keep it under about 20 seconds, because there is usually a queue of guisers at a busy door.

faqs.question: When is Auld Hallowe'en?
faqs.answer: Auld Hallowe'en is 11 November, the Old Style calendar date for 31 October. That is Wednesday 11 November 2026 and Thursday 11 November 2027.

faqs.question: What is a neep lantern made from?
faqs.answer: A neep lantern is a hollowed neep, the Scots word for a turnip or swede, with a face cut through and a candle inside. An 1890 Ayrshire sketch already describes boys carrying turnip lanterns on Halloween.

faqs.question: What does dooking mean in Scotland?
faqs.answer: Dooking means ducking, and at Halloween it means lifting a floating apple out of a tub of water with your mouth alone. On Tiree in the 19th century a silver sixpence also sat on the bottom of the tub.

faqs.question: How do you play treacle scones at Halloween?
faqs.answer: Spread scones with black treacle, hang them on strings from a line at head height, and have players eat them with their hands behind their backs. We found no early dated record of the game, so treat it as a later party tradition.

faqs.question: What happens in Robert Burns' poem Halloween?
faqs.answer: Written in 1785, it follows country people near the River Doon in Ayrshire through the night's fortune games: pulling kail stalks, burning nuts in pairs and choosing between three dishes. It is affectionate comedy, and a 1736 Caithness church record shows kail-pulling was already being reported decades earlier.

faqs.question: When is the Paisley Halloween Festival in 2026?
faqs.answer: Renfrewshire Council lists Friday 23 October 2026 from 4pm to 9pm and Saturday 24 October 2026 from 2pm to 9pm at Abbey Close, with a 400-strong parade each night from 7pm. The 2027 dates had not been published on 14 October 2026.

faqs.question: Where is the Samhuinn Fire Festival held in Edinburgh?
faqs.answer: The Beltane Fire Society holds Samhuinn on Calton Hill, on Saturday 31 October in 2026, with tickets sold only through Citizen Ticket. Some older guides still place it on the Royal Mile.

faqs.question: What was Carryanchor Night?
faqs.answer: It was a Burghead, Moray custom on the night before Halloween, when young people banged on doors with dried seaweed stalks called carryanchors and ran off. Two women recorded it for the School of Scottish Studies in 1985, and it was published in Scottish Studies in 1993.

# Halloween in Scotland: Guising, Neep Lanterns and Old Customs

Halloween in Scotland falls on 31 October, a Saturday in 2026 and a Sunday in 2027, and its defining custom is guising: children in disguise knock on doors and must perform a joke, song or rhyme, their party piece, before they get a treat. Around it sit neep (turnip) lanterns, dooking for apples, treacle scones on a string and the fortune games in Robert Burns' 1785 poem "Halloween".

If you are sending Halloween to someone in Scotland from elsewhere, two SubhSandesh platform figures apply: 38.5% of creators password-protect their page before sharing it, and a shared page averages 11.1 views. Neither is Halloween data, because none exists yet. Below are seven customs, each dated to the earliest record we could read, six original party pieces, and event dates for 2026 and 2027.

## What is Halloween called in Scotland?

Halloween in Scotland is the eve of Hallowday, All Saints' Day on 1 November, and Scots have long written it Hallowe'en. The [Scottish National Dictionary entry for Hallow (first published 1960)](https://dsl.ac.uk/entry/snd/hallow_n2) also records "Hallaleen" in Angus, Edinburgh, Dumfries and Glasgow speech.

The same entry notes Auld Hallowe'en, kept on 11 November under the Old Style calendar, and a Hallow Fair on 1 November that in Edinburgh was a cattle market.

In the Gaelic west the season was Samhain. John Gregorson Campbell, minister of Tiree, whose notebooks run from 1861 to 1891, saw children build one bonfire per house, the Samhnagan, and judged them "the natural and defiant welcome of the season" rather than the relic of a fire god.

## 7 Scottish Halloween traditions, dated from the record

Each entry gives the same four facts in the same order: what it is, the earliest dated record we read, where, and whether it survives.

### 1. Guising and the party piece

**What it is:** children go door to door in disguise and earn their treat by performing. **Earliest record:** the [Scottish National Dictionary entry for guiser](https://dsl.ac.uk/entry/snd/snd00072227) quotes Edinburgh boys out as "guizards" at Auld Yule in 1773, and an 1825 Hogmanay troupe acting a short play in which a hero called Goloshin is killed and revived by a doctor. **Where:** all of Scotland, once at Christmas Eve and Hogmanay as well as Halloween. **Today:** alive on 31 October, with the play shrunk to a joke or a song.

### 2. Neep lanterns

**What it is:** a hollowed neep (turnip or swede) with a face cut through and a candle inside. **Earliest record:** an 1890 Ayrshire sketch quoted in the dictionary's Hallow entry shows boys running about with false faces "and their bits o' turnip lanthrons" in their hands. **Where:** Lowlands and beyond; a 1954 Fife Herald line has a man slicing the inside out of a neep for one. **Today:** carved at home and in schools, though pumpkins are easier on the wrists.

### 3. Dooking for apples

**What it is:** lifting a floating apple out of a tub of water with your mouth alone. **Earliest record:** an 1828 Scots novel quoted in the Hallow entry lists "douking for apples, burning nuts, pulling kail-runts" as Halloween play. **Where:** everywhere; on Tiree, [Campbell's 1902 Witchcraft and Second Sight in the Highlands and Islands](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/58894) adds a silver sixpence on the bottom of the tub, to be lifted "without using his teeth". **Today:** still played at Halloween parties, often by dropping a fork from the teeth instead.

### 4. Treacle scones on a string

**What it is:** scones spread with black treacle, hung from a line at head height and eaten with your hands behind your back. **Earliest record:** none that we could date; it is absent from Campbell's notes and from every dictionary quotation we read. **Where:** kitchens, schools and church halls. **Today:** alive; we treat it as a later party game, not an old rite.

### 5. Pulling kail stocks and burning nuts

**What it is:** fortune games about sweethearts. A kale stalk pulled blindfold foretells a spouse's height and shape, soil on the root means money, and two named nuts on the fire tell whether a pair will burn together or jump apart. **Earliest record:** a 1736 Caithness church record in the Hallow entry reports one Thomas Harper "for Kaill-plucking, superstitiously, on Halloweve". **Where:** Ayrshire in Burns, Tiree in Campbell, Caithness in the kirk record. **Today:** rare; Campbell already said these divinations "left an abiding impression on few minds".

Burns also stages the three-dish test, which Campbell describes as clean water, dirty water and an empty plate, picked blindfold:

> In order, on the clean hearth-stane,
> The luggies three are ranged;

### 6. Hallow fires

**What it is:** a bonfire on Halloween night. **Earliest record:** a 1795 Statistical Account entry for a Perthshire parish, quoted in the Hallow entry, describes heath, broom and flax tied to a pole, lit, and carried at a run around the village on 31 October Old Style. **Where:** Perthshire, and Tiree, where "it was an object of ambition who should have the biggest". **Today:** public bonfires in Scotland now cluster on Bonfire Night, 5 November.

### 7. Carryanchor Night in Burghead

**What it is:** on the night before Halloween, young people in Burghead, Moray, banged on doors with a dried seaweed stalk, the carryanchor, then ran. **Earliest record:** two Burghead women recorded in 1985 for the School of Scottish Studies archive (tape SA 1985/136), published by [Margaret Bennett and Emily Lyle in Scottish Studies volume 31 (1993)](https://open.journals.ed.ac.uk/ScottishStudies/article/view/619). **Where:** Burghead; in Elgin, children instead toured the shops on Halloween shouting "Eelie-o-lo-lo gie's nuts". **Today:** we found no later record; the matching nights are Friday 30 October 2026 and Saturday 30 October 2027.

The women remembered groups of six to eight children, "never any singing or rhyme", and neighbours who put off repainting their doors until after Carryanchor Night. That makes it the only custom here that asked for nothing in return.

## Scottish Halloween customs compared: the oldest dated records

This table compares five customs by the earliest dated record we read, its region and the night.

| Custom | Earliest dated record we read | Region of that record | Night |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kail-pulling | 1736 church record | Caithness | 31 October |
| Guising | 1773 newspaper; Halloween by 1955 | Edinburgh; Galloway | 31 October (once also Yule, Hogmanay) |
| Hallow fire | 1795 Statistical Account | Perthshire | 31 October Old Style (11 November) |
| Turnip lantern | 1890 sketch | Ayrshire | 31 October |
| Carryanchor | 1985 archive tape | Burghead, Moray | 30 October |

The fortune games carry the oldest paper trail, and the turnip lantern, the symbol most guides open with, has the youngest dated mention of the four classic customs.

## 6 original party pieces for guising

A party piece should take under 20 seconds, because a guiser at a busy door has a queue behind them. These are our own lines, written for this page, and all are safe for children.

Jokes:

- Why did the neep lantern fail its exam? It couldnae get its heid round the questions.
- What did the treacle scone say to the guiser? "Hang on, I'll be right with you."
- Why do apples dread Halloween in Scotland? Every year they get a right dookin'.
- Why did the skeleton stay in on Hallowe'en? The haar went straight through him.

Rhymes:

- Hallowe'en, the nicht is cauld, / Our neep is lit, our joke is tauld; / A sweetie here, an apple there, / And we'll be off to the next stair.
- Knock, knock, a guiser in a sheet; / I've done my turn, now gie's a treat.

The 1923 Aberdeen rhyme in the Hallow entry ends "Up, and gie's oor Halloween!", so asking outright has a long pedigree. Doing the turn first is the Scottish part.

## Halloween events in Scotland: 2026 and 2027 dates

Two public events carry Scottish Halloween for crowds now. Dates were checked on 14 October 2026.

- **Paisley Halloween Festival.** [Renfrewshire Council's festival page](https://www.renfrewshire.gov.uk/parks-libraries-and-culture/events/paisley-halloween-festival) lists Friday 23 October 2026, 4pm to 9pm, and Saturday 24 October 2026, 2pm to 9pm, at Abbey Close. A 400-strong parade leaves at 7pm each night and takes about 60 minutes, and covered grandstand seats are £15 each or £54 for four. The 2027 dates were not published.
- **Samhuinn Fire Festival, Edinburgh.** The [Beltane Fire Society's 2026 ticket notice](https://beltane.org/2026/09/08/your-samhuinn-fire-festival-2026-tickets-are-now-on-sale/) puts it on Calton Hill on Saturday 31 October 2026, ticketed through Citizen Ticket only. Older guides still place it on the Royal Mile. If it keeps 31 October, 2027's falls on a Sunday; nothing is announced.
- **Auld Hallowe'en.** Wednesday 11 November 2026 and Thursday 11 November 2027, for anyone who wants the Old Style date.

## Sending Halloween to someone in Scotland

A party piece can travel where a guiser cannot. On SubhSandesh, 48.3% of shared pages are opened on a phone and 90.9% of started pages are published and shared, platform-wide and not Halloween-specific.

For a quick one, the [interactive Halloween card with a carved pumpkin and a Boo License](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) takes about 5 minutes, holds up to six photos, and has the recipient knock three times and carve a jack-o'-lantern until your word glows. It is a pumpkin, not a neep, and its kids tone keeps the ghosts round and blushing with no gore.

For the party piece itself, the [premium Halloween page with a 60-second voice note](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) takes about 10 minutes. Record your joke or rhyme as the voice note, add up to 12 photos, set the unlock time to 31 October, and their one reply of up to 280 characters is emailed to you.

If the person is a partner you are apart from and Halloween is only the excuse, the [I miss you page for a partner far away](https://subhsandesh.in/missyou-gf) says that more directly.

## When a link is the wrong way to mark Halloween in Scotland

Guising is a doorstep trade, and none of the 7 customs above works through a screen. A guiser on 31 October wants a sweetie in the bag, so fill the bowl first.

These pages greet one person; they are not party or school invitations. The interface is English only, so a Gaelic-speaking grandparent gets no Gaelic. And for someone in the same room, a treacle scone on a string beats anything we make.
